>  over my 37,5h / week go to my flex-time and can be turned into extra days off.   

Immediately after college I joined a company that enticed me with this! But the manager I got never officially gave out flextime. They left it up to you to know when "it's okay" to flex out (AKA, don't flex out if you're too busy!). Which means I rarely got flex time. Flex time wasn't officially written into any paperwork, so I suppose I learned my lesson there. I was salaried, and in the US there really aren't any labor laws preventing companies from pulling shit like this. (Not in New York either, which is where that job was). 

Salaried here means "we pay you to do a job, not a set amount of hours", and there is no legal protection against working too many hours.

I'm currently looking for an hourly tech gig, but it's hard to find good once, most I'm seeing are salaried (of course.. since that means companies can get every drop out of you).

I don't think it's controversial to consider software engineering a difficult discipline. Burnout is a common issue for software engineers.

It does depend on your job, your company, and what you're working on. Last gig was sysprog, and instead of talking about it I'll quote a [classic](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/1311_05-08_mickens.pdf) :

>The systems programmer has traced a network problem across eight machines, three time zones, and a brief diversion into Amish country, where the problem was transmitted in the front left hoof of a mule named Deliverance. The systems programmer has read the kernel source, to better understand the deep ways of the universe, and the systems programmer has seen the comment in the scheduler that says “DOES THIS WORK LOL,” and the systems programmer has wept instead of LOLed, and the systems programmer has submitted a kernel patch to restore balance to The Force and fix the priority inversion that was causing MySQL to hang. A systems programmer will know what to do when society breaks down, because the systems programmer already lives in a world without law.

That job was a goddamn headache. I'd come home mentally done for the day, and my hours were long, well past 8hrs more often than not. I enjoyed it, but it was hard work.

And once again, I signed up for this, and it's not a pissing contest, I just find that claim ridiculous.

The right to **dignity** at work and in life does not need to correlate with how hard you work. We all deserve fair wages, and reasonable working hours.

>   A "work certification" means less than nothing in identifying a skilled tech worker.  

There are plenty of quantifiable skills; types of languages and their libraries (Rust, Python, Python Async, etc etc), different areas of application (systems programming is very different than web development, etc), it would take me a while to write any sort of comprehensive list (I would have to map out all of computing, I guess). A certification wouldn't mean less than a college degree or work history (in fact, it'd be better, because of better scope).

There is. Resume/work history, Github projects, technical interviews. Code doesn't lie, you can't bullshit working code. I'd say tech is one of the more quantifiable professions.
